title: Biomechanics Gurus need to SHUT UP about Optimal Training
summary: NH attacks 'biomechanics gurus' who label the big three and other compound lifts as suboptimal for hypertrophy due to a poor stimulus-to-fatigue ratio. He argues they misunderstand the concept (fatigue and stimulus are linked), that machines carry their own injury risks and less total stimulus, that tendons need loading for longevity, and that babying lifters lowers their ceiling.
claims: There is no single optimal way to train; exercise value is case by case and one-size-fits-all methods rob people of thinking for themselves

Gurus target the big three because they are popular and drive clicks, then reverse-engineer reasons; you should start from the concept and find lifts that fit, not start with the deadlift and argue it is bad
Criticising any lift is easy; that does not make it intellectually honest
Losing balance, losing your brace or good-morning-ing the weight are not reasons the squat is bad; they are technique faults the lifter must fix
He has done tens of thousands of squats and never lost balance; balance and bracing are essential lifting and athletic skills
Stimulus-to-fatigue ratio is simple: every lift gives fatigue and stimulus; fatigue is what turns into stimulus, so less fatigue also means less stimulus
Compound lifts may give more of both fatigue and stimulus; they are only worse if the excess fatigue overtakes the excess stimulus
Machines can injure too: they are built for one body type and fixed path, so a lifter with different limb lengths can get overuse injuries from a bad angle
Free weights let you adapt your body around the bar; they take practice but you will lift for 10 years anyway
People who start on machines and cables because barbells intimidate them often never progress to free weights and stay small
Machines let you lift much more load than the free-weight equivalent because the machine does part of the work, so per unit of load they give less of both fatigue and stimulus
A deadlift only has a bad ratio if you do too much volume; that is your programming problem, not the lift's
Advanced lifters use machines as a complement, never as the foundation; staying in the machine 'baby playground' means never learning fatigue management
Tendons and the spine exist to be loaded; avoiding loading does not save 'tendon capital' but leaves untrained tendons that fail in old age
Joint replacements later in life happen to people who push the limits and accumulate too much fatigue, not to bodybuilders who manage fatigue
Saying lifters lack the skill to train close to failure on squat, bench and deadlift is the bigotry of low expectations; the Pygmalion effect means treating people as incapable lowers their ceiling
Squat, bench and deadlift are movement patterns; condemning them condemns all their variations (Larsen press, close-grip bench, RDLs, stiff-leg deadlifts, front squats), leaving only machines
Gurus swung the pendulum from too much big three to the opposite extreme; the balance is a majority of compound movements completed with machines, cables and isolation
Natural bodybuilders before PEDs built their physiques with compound movements, and people with great physiques today still mostly do
Isolation without compounds is like the cherry without the cake
Many biomechanics gurus have unimpressive physiques, suggesting their methods do not work or they do not use them; time-tested methods survive while gimmicks fade
